a: These too are Solomon's proverbs
p: The heading opens a new collection, chapters 25–29, and ties it back to the Solomon sayings of 10:1–22:16.
b: "These too" (gam 'elleh) looks back: like the sayings that began at 10:1, these are "proverbs of Solomon" (on mashal, "proverb", see 1:1). The same words, "these too", open the short appendix at 24:23. Chapters 25–29 hold 137 verses after the heading, and scholars commonly divide them in two: 25–27, rich in pictures from nature and farm life, with many "like X, so Y" comparisons, and 28–29, mostly two-line contrasts between the righteous and the wicked, with much about rulers. The heading claims the sayings are Solomon's but were handed on by others. Solomon was remembered for three thousand proverbs (1 Kings 4:32); the heading does not say these were all of them, or that Hezekiah's men added none of their own.

a: copied
p: The verb he'tiqu means "moved" or "transferred": the sayings were carried over from one place to another.
b: He'tiqu comes from 'ataq, "move, shift". Abram "moved on" from one camp to another with this verb (Genesis 12:8), God moves mountains with it (Job 9:5), and words "have moved off" from Job's friends (Job 32:15). Applied to sayings, it means they were transferred: from older scrolls into a new one, or from memory and speech into writing. In later Hebrew he'tiq is the ordinary word for copying a text, and also for translating one. The Greek has exegrapsanto, "copied out". Either way the verb describes editors and scribes at work on material they received, not authors writing new sayings. It is the only place in the Bible that names a team of copyists and says when they worked.

a: the men of Hezekiah king of Judah
p: Hezekiah ruled Judah about 715–687 BC. His court had a secretary and a recorder, and reasons to gather old wisdom.
b: Kings names two of Hezekiah's literate officials: "Shebna the secretary and Joah son of Asaph, the recorder" (2 Kings 18:18). "The men of" a king are his officials and servants. Several things make a collecting project in his reign likely. After the northern kingdom fell to Assyria in 722 BC, refugees came south, and Judah became the keeper of Israel's traditions. Writing spread widely in eighth-century Judah: inscriptions, seals and the Siloam tunnel inscription survive from this time. Kings and Chronicles present Hezekiah as a reformer who did "what was right in the LORD's eyes" (2 Kings 18:3), restored worship "with the words of David and of Asaph" (2 Chronicles 29:30), and held a Passover like none "since the days of Solomon" (2 Chronicles 30:26). Gathering Solomon's sayings fits that picture of a king reviving the age of David and Solomon. Most commentators, including critical ones, take the note as a plausible memory of real scribal work.

a: Hezekiah king of Judah
t: Hezekiah and his company in Jewish tradition
p: The Talmud credits "Hezekiah and his company" with writing down Isaiah, Proverbs, the Song of Songs and Ecclesiastes.
b: A famous passage on who wrote the books of the Bible (Bava Batra 15a) says that "Hezekiah and his company" wrote Isaiah, Proverbs, the Song of Songs and Ecclesiastes. The rabbis did not mean that Hezekiah composed Proverbs. They meant that his circle gave these books their written form, which is close to what 25:1 itself says. The tradition treats 25:1 as a picture of careful scholars handing on a sacred text, a model for later teachers.

a: The glory of God is to keep a matter hidden
p: God's greatness shows in what he keeps hidden; a king's greatness shows in getting to the bottom of things.
b: The saying sets God and kings side by side, using the same word for "matter" in each line. God's ways and the depths of the world are beyond human reach (Deuteronomy 29:29; Job 11:7; Job 28). A king, by contrast, earns honor by investigating: hearing cases, uncovering the truth and judging rightly, as Solomon did with the two mothers (1 Kings 3:16–28). The next verse adds that a king's own heart is beyond searching too. Glendon Bryce and Raymond Van Leeuwen showed that "glory" and "search" come back in 25:27, so 25:2–27 forms a small, deliberate unit, probably a lesson for young men who would serve at court. Francis Bacon made the verse famous in English, reading it as a charter for scientific inquiry: God hides the secrets of nature so that people may have the honor of finding them out.

a: Clear the slag from the silver
p: The same verb "clear" opens 25:4 and 25:5: purifying silver pictures purifying a king's court.
b: Hebrew hago, "remove, clear away", begins both verses, and the Plain repeats "clear" to show the pairing. A smith heats silver ore and skims off the slag, the impure waste, so that clean metal remains for a vessel. In the same way, removing wicked advisers leaves a throne that stands "in righteousness". The image of refining for moral testing runs through the Bible (17:3; 27:21; Psalm 12:6; Isaiah 1:22–25; Malachi 3:2–3). The Greek translator turned both verbs into blunt commands, "strike" the silver and "kill" the ungodly before the king (see the variant). On the throne made firm by righteousness, see 16:12 and 29:14.

a: Do not claim honor for yourself before a king
t: "Come up here" and Jesus' parable of the seats
p: Jesus' advice about choosing the lowest seat at a wedding (Luke 14:8–11) echoes this saying closely.
b: The courtier who pushes forward risks being moved down in public; the one who waits may be called up. Jesus gives the same counsel at a meal: take the last place, so that the host may say, "Friend, come up higher," and then you will be honored before the guests (Luke 14:8–10). He ends with a wider principle: everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and the one who humbles himself will be exalted (Luke 14:11). Rabbinic teachers used the verse the same way. Leviticus Rabbah (1:5) has Rabbi Akiva teach in the name of Simeon ben Azzai: go down two or three seats from your place, because it is better to be told "come up" than "go down". The saying also anticipates 29:23.

a: whom your eyes have seen
t: Which verse do these words belong to?
p: The Hebrew verse ends "whom your eyes have seen". Many modern versions move the words to start 25:8.
b: The Masoretic Text places "whom your eyes have seen" at the end of 25:7, where it describes the noble: you are humiliated in front of someone you saw, someone who knows you. The KJV follows this. But the phrase is awkward there, and the Greek reads "speak what your eyes have seen" as its own command. Many modern versions join the words to 25:8: what you have seen, do not rush to bring to court. That fits the theme of 25:8–10 (careless lawsuits and testimony), but it goes against the verse division and accents of the Hebrew. The Plain keeps the Hebrew division.

a: argue a case
t: A lawsuit, not just a quarrel
p: Rib is a legal dispute, a case brought before judges or elders at the town gate.
b: Rib (here and in 25:9, "your dispute") is the standard word for a lawsuit or formal complaint, though it can also mean a quarrel. In Israel such cases were heard by the elders at the town gate (Deuteronomy 21:19; Ruth 4:1–2). The advice is practical: rushing into court may end with the other side proving you wrong in public. The better course is to settle the matter directly with your neighbor (25:9). Jesus gives similar advice: make terms with your opponent on the way to court (Matthew 5:25), and go and correct a brother who wrongs you "with just the two of you there" (Matthew 18:15).

a: disgrace you
t: A rare word that looks like hesed
p: The verb here is built on the same letters as hesed, "loyal love", but it means the opposite: to shame.
b: Yechassedkha comes from a root chsd that in Hebrew usually gives hesed, "loyal love". A second, rarer root with the same letters means "shame, disgrace", as in Leviticus 20:17, where an incestuous union is called "a disgrace" (chesed), and probably 14:34, where sin brings shame (chesed) to peoples. Most dictionaries count two separate roots. The person who betrays a secret in court (25:9) will be shamed by whoever hears it, and the bad name (dibbah, "report, slander") will stick.

a: Golden apples set in silver
p: The picture is of gold ornaments shaped like fruit, set in a carved or filigree silver frame.
b: Tappuach is usually "apple" (Song of Songs 2:3), though some think of the apricot or quince. "Golden apples" are probably fruit-shaped ornaments of gold, not real fruit. Maskiyyot means carved work or images (Numbers 33:52; Ezekiel 8:12); here, a silver setting or filigree around the gold. The words "at the right moment" ('al-'ofnav) are uncertain. 'Ofen may be related to the word for "wheel", so some translate "on its wheels", meaning a word that runs smoothly or comes around at its proper time; others take it as "in its two parts", a well-balanced saying. Most agree the sense is a word that fits its occasion (compare 15:23).

a: Golden apples set in silver
p: Maimonides used this verse to explain how the Bible has an outer and an inner meaning.
b: In the introduction to The Guide of the Perplexed, Moses Maimonides (about 1190) took this verse as a picture of how a parable works. A golden apple is covered with silver filigree that has very small holes. Seen from a distance, it looks like a silver apple; looked at closely, the gold shows through. The outer meaning of a prophetic or wise saying, he said, is silver: valuable, useful for living well. Its inner meaning is gold: truth about God and the world. His reading shaped centuries of Jewish and Christian thinking about the levels of meaning in Scripture, though it reads more into the verse than the original saying, about well-timed speech, intended.

a: a chill of snow in harvest time
t: Snow at harvest: a cold drink, not a storm
p: Snow falling at harvest would be a disaster (26:1). Here it means snow brought down from the mountains to cool drinks.
b: The grain harvest in Israel comes in late spring and early summer, when there is no snow or rain (compare 26:1; 1 Samuel 12:17). The saying cannot mean a snowfall, which would ruin the crop. It probably refers to snow or ice carried from Mount Hermon or Lebanon and stored to cool drinks for workers in the heat. A trustworthy messenger is that refreshing to the master who sent him; the lazy or wicked messengers of 10:26, 13:17 and 26:6 are the opposite. The Greek reads "as a going-out of snow in harvest helps against the heat", which shows the translator understood it the same way. In Swete's apparatus, Codex Vaticanus has only "a going-out" and Codices Sinaiticus and Alexandrinus only "snow".

a: Clouds and wind, and yet no rain
p: Jude uses the same picture for false teachers: "waterless clouds swept along by winds" (Jude 12).
b: In a dry land, wind and gathering clouds raise the hope of rain, and nothing comes. The man who promises gifts and never gives them raises hope the same way. Jude borrows the image for teachers who promise much and give nothing: "They are waterless clouds swept along by winds" (Jude 12). The word for clouds here, nesi'im, sounds like nasi', "leader, prince", and some readers hear a hint at rulers who promise and do not deliver.

a: a soft tongue breaks bone
p: The paradox of a soft tongue breaking something hard has a close parallel in the Words of Ahiqar.
b: "Bone" (garem) is the hardest part of the body. A soft, patient word, the saying claims, can break resistance that force cannot. The first line fits the court: a ruler is not won over by pressure but by "slowness to anger" ('orekh 'appayim, "length of nostrils", the same phrase used of God in Exodus 34:6). The Aramaic Words of Ahiqar, set at the Assyrian court of Sennacherib and Esarhaddon (Hezekiah's own era) and copied at Elephantine in Egypt in the 400s BC, has a striking parallel: a king's speech is soft, yet it breaks the ribs of a dragon (as Lindenberger translates the line). The two sayings probably share an international courtly tradition, not direct borrowing. Compare 15:1.

a: too much of it
t: Too much honey, too much of you
p: The same verb, "have too much of", links 25:16 and 25:17: honey you overeat, and a neighbor you overvisit.
b: Saba' means to be full or satisfied, and also to be fed up. In 25:16 you have too much honey and throw it up; in 25:17 your neighbor has too much of you and comes to hate you. The two sayings were placed together because of the shared verb. Honey comes back at 25:27, and the pairing is a gentle lesson in limits: good things, sweet food and friendship alike, are spoiled by excess. On honey in Proverbs, see 24:13 and 27:7.
orig: פֶּן־תִּשְׂבָּעֶנּוּ (pen-tisba'ennu), 'or you will be sated with it'

a: as a lying witness
t: The ninth commandment as a weapon
p: The second line uses the very words of the commandment against false witness (Exodus 20:16).
b: The words 'oneh vere'ehu 'ed shaqer repeat the commandment: "You must not testify against your neighbor as a lying witness" (Exodus 20:16; Deuteronomy 5:20). The saying gives the commandment a picture. A false witness in court is a club, a sword and a sharpened arrow, because in Israel a false accusation could cost a person property, freedom or life (Deuteronomy 19:16–21; 1 Kings 21:10–13). Proverbs returns to the false witness often (6:19; 12:17; 14:5; 19:5, 9; 21:28).

a: vinegar poured on soda
p: Neter is natron, a natural soda. Vinegar fizzes on it and spoils it, like cheerful songs sung to a grieving person.
b: Neter is natron, a sodium carbonate mined around the salt lakes of Egypt and used as soap (Jeremiah 2:22). Vinegar on it foams and makes it useless. The KJV's "nitre" is the old word for the same mineral. The point is a reaction that is wrong for the moment: taking away someone's coat on a cold day, and singing happy songs to someone in grief (compare Romans 12:15, "weep along with those who weep"). The Greek translator read the line differently, as "vinegar on a wound", and some modern versions follow it (see the variant). The first line, "Pulling off someone's coat", is missing in the Greek, and some scholars think it was copied by mistake from the similar-looking last words of 25:19.

a: someone who hates you
t: Not just "enemy" but "the one who hates you"
p: The Hebrew says "the one who hates you", the same word the law uses when it commands help for a hater's donkey.
b: Most English versions say "your enemy", and that is the sense, but the Hebrew word is sone'akha, "the one who hates you", a personal enemy, not a foreign army. The law already asked for practical kindness to such a person: "If you see the donkey of someone who hates you lying down under its load, hold back from leaving him alone with it" (Exodus 23:5; compare Exodus 23:4). Job swears he was never glad when "someone who hated me was ruined" (Job 31:29), and Proverbs forbids gloating over an enemy's fall (24:17–18) and taking revenge (20:22; 24:29). This saying goes one step further: feed him. The Greek renders "your enemy" (ho echthros sou), and Paul quotes the Greek (Romans 12:20).

a: scooping up burning coals onto his head
p: The verb chotheh means to scoop up or carry fire. "Heap" comes from the Greek translation.
b: Chotheh is used of taking fire from a hearth (Isaiah 30:14) and, in a related sense, of God snatching someone away (Psalm 52:5). It pictures picking up glowing coals, as with a pan or shovel, and placing them on someone's head. The familiar "heap coals of fire" comes from the Greek soreuseis, "you will pile up", which Paul quotes (Romans 12:20) and the KJV follows. Coals on the head appear nowhere else in the Hebrew Bible. Burning coals are usually signs of judgment (Psalm 11:6; Psalm 140:10), which is why the meaning of this verse is so debated; see the next note and the chapter page.
orig: גֶחָלִים אַתָּה חֹתֶה (gechalim 'attah chotheh), 'coals you are scooping'

a: burning coals onto his head
p: The coals have been read as shame that leads to repentance, as added punishment, or as an Egyptian penitence rite.
b: Shame and repentance. Kindness makes the enemy feel his guilt so sharply that it burns, and he turns into a friend. Augustine called the coals "burning groans of repentance", and most Christian readers have followed him. Punishment. If he does not repent, your kindness adds to his judgment, since coals elsewhere mean wrath (Psalm 140:10). Chrysostom mentioned this reading while urging that Paul's real goal was reconciliation. An Egyptian ritual. Siegfried Morenz pointed to a Demotic Egyptian tale in which a penitent carries a pan of burning coals on his head to show remorse; the saying would then mean that kindness brings the enemy to public repentance. William Klassen surveyed the readings and favored a sign of repentance. The final line, "the LORD will pay you back", keeps the reward in God's hands either way.

a: the LORD will pay you back
t: "He will make him at peace with you"
p: The Talmud rereads yeshallem lakh, "he will repay you", as "he will make him at peace with you".
b: Yeshallem, "he will repay", comes from the same root as shalom, "peace". The Talmud (Sukkah 52a) applies the saying to the evil inclination, the enemy inside: if it is hungry, feed it the bread of Torah; if thirsty, give it the water of Torah. Then it plays on the last word: do not read only "he will repay you" (yeshallem lakh), but "he will make him at peace with you" (yashlimennu lakh). The Greek adds "with good things": "the Lord will repay you with good things." Paul's quotation in Romans 12:20 stops before this line; he has already said that repaying belongs to God (Romans 12:19, quoting Deuteronomy 32:35).

a: for you will be scooping up burning coals onto his head
p: Paul quotes the Greek of 25:21–22 almost word for word, then adds his own conclusion: conquer evil with good.
b: Paul writes: "If your enemy hungers, feed him; if he thirsts, give him drink, for by doing this you will pile coals of fire on his head" (Romans 12:20, rendered from the Greek). His wording follows the Greek of Proverbs closely, with three differences: his opening "rather", the closing promise he leaves out, and the verb for "feed". The Greek (Rahlfs) has trephe; Paul has psomize, which is also the reading of Codex Vaticanus. Two things frame the quotation in Romans. Before it, Paul tells believers never to take revenge but to make room for the anger (Romans 12:19). After it, he sums up: "Do not be defeated by evil. Defeat evil with good" (Romans 12:21). Dunn and Moo take Paul to mean that kindness aims to win the enemy; some think he also leaves judgment open if the enemy refuses. Paul sets the old saying beside Jesus' command to love enemies (Matthew 5:44).

a: The north wind brings forth rain
t: A north wind that brings rain?
p: In Israel the north wind usually brings clear, cold weather, so this line has puzzled readers since ancient times.
b: Rain in Israel comes from the west, off the Mediterranean (1 Kings 18:44; Luke 12:54). The KJV took the line to mean the north wind "driveth away rain", but the verb techolel means "brings forth, gives birth to". Several explanations are offered: the saying came from a place where a north wind does bring rain; tsafon here means the northwest; or the saying values the sound-play over weather. Tsafon, "north", comes from a root meaning "hidden", and the second line speaks of a tongue of seter, "secrecy", one that talks in secret. As surely as that wind brings a storm, gossip behind someone's back brings angry faces.

a: Living in a corner up on the roof is better
p: This saying repeats 21:9. Hezekiah's men copied some sayings already in the first Solomon collection.
b: Flat roofs in Israel were used as living space (1 Samuel 9:25–26; 2 Kings 4:10), but a corner of the roof is a cramped, exposed place, open to sun and rain. The Hebrew of 25:24 and 21:9 differs by one letter. Several such repeats in 25–29 suggest that the scribes worked from a source that overlapped with the earlier collection, and did not remove the doubles (compare 26:22 with 18:8, 27:13 with 20:16, and 28:6 with 19:1). Sayings about a quarrelsome wife (19:13; 21:19; 27:15–16) are addressed to young men choosing a wife; on how they portray women, see the note on 27:15.

a: a righteous person who totters in front of the wicked
p: A spring muddied by trampling feet is useless to the thirsty. So is a righteous person who gives way.
b: Nirpas means "trampled, fouled by feet" (Ezekiel 32:2; 34:18–19, where animals foul the water with their feet). A spring or well was life to a village. The mouth of the righteous is meant to be "a spring of life" (10:11). When such a person "totters" (mat, the word for slipping feet, Psalm 15:5; Psalm 55:22) before the wicked, whether by giving in to pressure, losing a case or being bought, the community's source of good is fouled. The image fits a courtroom, where a righteous judge or witness who yields to the powerful poisons justice for everyone.

a: searching out their glory is glory
t: A line nobody is sure of
p: The Hebrew literally reads "and searching their glory is glory". Translators have rebuilt the line in many ways.
b: The first line is clear: too much honey is bad. The second, vecheqer kevodam kavod, is not. The Plain keeps the Masoretic wording. Three main readings exist. (1) The "not" of the first line also governs the second: it is not glorious to seek one's own glory (KJV, many modern versions). (2) The line reverses the first: searching out weighty matters (kavod also means "weight") is honorable, picking up 25:2, "the glory of kings is searching a matter out". (3) The text is damaged and should be emended, for example to "and to seek weighty words is to be sated". Bryce and Van Leeuwen note that "glory" and "search" both close the unit that 25:2 opened, which favors some link to 25:2. The Greek has "but one should honor glorious words" (see the variant).

a: a person who cannot rein in his own spirit
t: A city with its wall broken down
p: A man without self-control is as open to attack as a city whose wall has been breached.
b: An ancient city lived or died by its wall. Once a wall was breached (perutsah, "broken through", as at Nehemiah 1:3; 2:13), anyone could walk in. A person who has no "restraint" (ma'tsar) on his spirit, his temper and impulses, is open to every enemy, inside and out. The saying is the reverse of 16:32, where the one who rules his spirit is better than one who captures a city. Christian writers linked it with self-control as a fruit of the Spirit (Galatians 5:23).
orig: אֵין מַעְצָר לְרוּחוֹ ('ein ma'tsar leruho), 'no restraint for his spirit'

a: Honor is as out of place for a fool
t: Snow in summer, rain at harvest
p: Both are unnatural in Israel's climate, and rain at harvest could destroy a crop.
b: Israel's summer is dry and hot; snow then is unthinkable. Rain at the grain harvest was rare enough to be a sign from God, as when Samuel called down thunder and rain on the wheat harvest to rebuke the people for asking for a king (1 Samuel 12:17–18). Honor (kavod, also "weight") given to a fool is just as unnatural, and as damaging. The first twelve verses of the chapter are a string of sayings on the kesil, the fool, the commonest fool word in Proverbs (see 1:22). Honor for the fool frames the opening (26:1, 26:8), and the series ends with someone worse than a fool (26:12).

a: a curse that has no cause does not land
p: The written Hebrew says the curse does "not" come; the Hebrew read aloud says it comes "to him", perhaps the curser.
b: Hebrew lo' ("not") and lo ("to him") sound alike. The written text (Ketiv) has "not": an undeserved curse flutters about like a bird and never settles on its target. The reading tradition (Qere) has "to him", which can mean the curse comes back on the one who spoke it. The Plain follows the Ketiv with most modern versions and the Greek ("a vain curse will come upon no one"); see the variant. Curses were feared as real powers in the ancient world. The saying reassures the innocent that a curse without cause has no power, as Balaam found when he could not curse Israel (Numbers 23:8), and as David trusted when Shimei cursed him (2 Samuel 16:5–12).

a: a rod for fools' backs
p: The rod (shevet) here is a stick for beating, as plainly as the whip is for the horse.
b: The verse is a list: each creature is driven by its own tool. Meteg is the bridle or bit, the same word God uses when he puts his "bridle" on the lips of Assyria's king (2 Kings 19:28). The shevet, rod or stick, is for the backs of fools. Proverbs says the same in 10:13 ("for the back of one with no sense there is a rod") and 19:29. In Israel's law, judges could order a beating of up to forty blows for certain wrongs (Deuteronomy 25:1–3). The saying treats the fool as an animal who will not respond to words, only to pain; the next sayings (26:4–12) show how hard it is to deal with him any other way. On the rod in raising children, see 29:15.

a: Don't answer a fool in line with his folly
t: Two sayings that seem to contradict each other
p: 26:4 says do not answer a fool; 26:5 says answer him. Side by side, they teach that the wise must judge the situation.
b: The two sayings use almost the same words with opposite commands, and someone put them next to each other on purpose. The reasons differ: answer, and you may become like the fool (26:4); do not answer, and he will think himself wise (26:5). Readers have resolved the tension in several ways. Different subjects: the Talmud (Shabbat 30b) says one verse is about matters of Torah and the other about worldly matters. Different situations: most modern commentators (Kidner, Fox, Waltke) say the pair shows that no rule works every time; wisdom is knowing when to speak and when to keep silent (compare Ecclesiastes 3:7). Different manners: do not answer in the fool's way, with his insults and anger, but do answer as his folly deserves, by exposing it. The pairing itself teaches what the whole book assumes: proverbs are tools to be used with judgment, not laws (26:7, 9).

a: in line with his folly
p: The little word ke- can mean "in the manner of" or "as it deserves". The two sayings use both senses.
b: Ke'ivvalto is "like his folly, according to his folly". In 26:4 the natural sense is "on his level": do not argue the way a fool argues, or you join him. In 26:5 the natural sense is "as his folly calls for": give the answer that shows his folly for what it is, or he will think himself wise. The Plain uses "in line with his folly" in both verses so that the reader can see the same Hebrew and feel the difference. 'Ivvelet, "folly", is the stubborn folly of the 'evil (see 1:7), here attached to the kesil, the dull fool. Paul uses the second sense when he boasts "as a fool" to answer boasters in Corinth: "I have become a fool! You forced me to it" (2 Corinthians 12:11).

a: Answer a fool in line with his folly
t: Why the rabbis almost hid Proverbs
p: The Talmud says some sages wanted to withdraw Proverbs from use because of this pair of verses.
b: The Talmud (Shabbat 30b) reports that the sages wanted to "hide away" (lignoz) the book of Proverbs, as they had considered doing with Ecclesiastes, "because its words contradict each other". The example given is 26:4–5. They kept it, the Talmud says, because the contradiction could be explained: "Answer" applies to matters of Torah, where an error must be corrected, and "Do not answer" to worldly matters. It illustrates the Torah case with Rabban Gamaliel, who answered a student mocking his teaching. To "hide away" a book meant to withdraw it from public reading, not necessarily to remove it from Scripture. The debate shows that the rabbis read Proverbs as one sacred book whose sayings had to agree.

a: drinks down violence
p: "Drinking violence" (shoteh chamas) is an idiom for taking in harm; sending a fool with a message invites it.
b: Chamas is violence or wrong done to someone. To "drink" it is to take it in fully, as one drinks injustice in Job 15:16 and scorn in Job 34:7. A messenger in the ancient world carried his master's words and acted for him (13:17; 25:13). Send a fool, and you cripple yourself, as if you cut off your own feet, and you swallow the damage he does. The Greek turns the line into a moral lesson: one who sends a message by a foolish messenger makes a reproach for himself from his own ways.

a: and a proverb in fools' mouths
t: A proverb is only as good as its user
p: 26:7 and 26:9 end with the same line: a proverb in a fool's mouth is useless (26:7) or dangerous (26:9).
b: The two lines are identical in Hebrew (umashal befi kesilim), and the Plain renders them the same way. In 26:7 the proverb hangs limp like a lame man's legs: a fool can quote it, but he cannot walk on it. In 26:9 it is a thorn in the hand of a drunk: he may hurt himself or others with it. These two sayings say something about the whole book. A proverb is not a magic formula. It takes wisdom to know which proverb fits which moment, as 26:4–5 just showed. The verb dalyu in 26:7 is an unusual form, probably from dalal, "hang down, dangle", though the form is odd enough that the KJV guessed "are not equal".

a: like tying the stone into the sling
t: A stone tied into a sling
p: A stone tied fast in a sling cannot be thrown: honor given to a fool is just as pointless, or it flies back.
b: Margemah, from ragam, "to stone", is most likely a sling. A slinger lays the stone loose in the pouch; tie it in, and the sling is useless or swings back at him. So is honoring a fool. Another old reading takes margemah as a heap of stones. Jerome's Latin Vulgate reads "like one who throws a stone onto the heap of Mercury", a roadside cairn where travelers added a stone in honor of the god. The same reading appears in the Talmud, which applies the verse to teaching an unworthy student: it is like throwing a stone to Markulis, that is, Mercury (Chullin 133a). Jerome probably learned it from his Jewish teachers. It makes honor for a fool a superstitious waste. Rashi and many medieval Jewish readers took it as a sling.

a: A thorn comes up in a drunkard's hand
t: A thorn in a drunk man's hand
p: Either a thorn sticks into a drunk's hand without his noticing, or he waves a thornbush around and hurts others.
b: The Hebrew says a thorn "goes up" or "comes up" ('alah) in the drunkard's hand. It may mean a thorn that pierces the hand of a man too drunk to feel it, or a thornbush he picks up and swings about. Both make sense of the second line: the fool may quote a proverb with no sense of what it means, or use it as a weapon. The Greek reads "thorns grow in the hand of a drunkard, and slavery in the hand of fools". On drunkenness in Proverbs, see 20:1 and 23:29–35.

a: An archer shooting at everyone in sight
p: Each of the verse's main words can be read more than one way, and translations differ widely.
b: Rav can mean "archer" (Jeremiah 50:29; Job 16:13), "master" or "great one". Mecholel can mean "wounding" or "bringing forth, forming". So the KJV has "The great God that formed all things both rewardeth the fool, and rewardeth transgressors", taking sokher as "rewards" (it means "hires") and 'overim as "transgressors" (it means "those passing by"). The Greek is different again: "All the flesh of fools endures much storm, for their frenzy is shattered." Most modern scholars read the archer: hiring a fool, or any stranger who happens by, is as dangerous as an archer shooting at random, because you cannot control the harm. That fits the theme of 26:6 (sending a message by a fool). The Plain follows it, but every reading of this verse is a guess.

a: A dog goes back to its vomit
t: 2 Peter 2:22: the dog and the sow
p: 2 Peter quotes this saying, but not in the Greek of Proverbs; it pairs it with a saying about a washed sow.
b: 2 Peter applies the proverb to teachers who knew the way of righteousness and turned back from it: "The word of the true proverb has happened to them: 'A dog that has turned back to its own vomit,' and, 'A sow that has washed, to wallowing in the mud'" (2 Peter 2:22, rendered from the Greek). The wording does not come from the Greek of Proverbs, which has emetos for vomit; 2 Peter uses exerama and a different verb for "turn back". The writer either translated the Hebrew directly or, more likely, used the saying as it circulated in his day. The sow saying is not in Proverbs at all. A close parallel appears in the Syriac Story of Ahiqar, where a wayward son is like a pig that went to the baths and then wallowed in a muddy pit. Bauckham suggests 2 Peter knew the two sayings already paired.

a: a fool does his folly over again
p: In Israel dogs were scavengers, not pets, so the picture is meant to disgust.
b: Dogs in the ancient Near East mostly roamed in packs and lived off refuse and corpses (1 Kings 14:11; 1 Kings 21:19; Psalm 59:6). To call someone a dog was an insult (1 Samuel 17:43; 2 Samuel 16:9). The image is not only that the fool repeats himself, but that he returns to what his own body threw out as harmful: he goes back to the very folly that made him sick. Shoneh, "repeating", is related to shanah, "do twice", the word behind Mishnah, "repetition" or "teaching", in a very different sense.

a: You see a man who is wise in his own eyes?
p: After eleven sayings against the fool, the series ends with someone worse: the man who is sure he is wise.
b: The fool at least might be taught or corrected; the self-satisfied man will not listen to anyone. "Wise in his own eyes" ties back to 26:5, where answering the fool is meant to keep him from becoming exactly this. The same warning appears in 3:7 and 28:11, and Isaiah pronounces a woe on those "wise in their own eyes" (Isaiah 5:21). Paul echoes the Greek of 3:7 when he tells the Romans not to be wise in their own estimation (Romans 12:16). The second line comes back word for word in 29:20, about a man hasty with words. In 26:16 the lazy one has the same problem.

a: A lion is out on the road!
p: This saying is close to 22:13: the lazy one invents a lion to avoid going out to work.
b: In 22:13 the lazy one says there is a lion outside and he will be killed in the streets. Here he says a lion is in the road, in the open squares. Two different words for lion are used, shachal and 'ari. Lions did live in Israel's thickets and hills (Judges 14:5; 1 Samuel 17:34; Amos 3:12), but not in town squares. The excuse is absurd on purpose. 26:13–16 is a little portrait of the lazy one ('atsel): he will not go out (26:13), will not get up (26:14), will not even feed himself (26:15), and thinks he is wiser than anyone (26:16).

a: The door turns on its pivot
t: Doors that swing on a pivot
p: Ancient doors turned on a post set into a stone socket, not on modern hinges.
b: A door in Israel hung on a post fixed at one edge of the door, which turned in a socket stone at the bottom and a hole at the top. Many socket stones survive from excavations. Tsir is that pivot. The joke is that the door moves and goes nowhere, and so does the lazy one: he turns over in bed and stays put.

a: The lazy one sinks his hand into the bowl
p: Repeats 19:24 with a small change at the end: he is too "weary" to bring his hand back to his mouth.
b: People ate from a common dish, dipping bread or their hands into it. The lazy one gets his hand into the bowl and cannot be bothered to lift it out again. In 19:24 he "cannot be bothered to lift it back to his mouth"; here "he is too weary" (nil'ah) to do it. The KJV's "bosom" (here and in 19:24) is an older guess for tsallachat, which means a dish (2 Kings 21:13). The exaggeration is the point: laziness that will not even feed itself.

a: than seven who can answer with good sense
p: Seven means a full number: the lazy one thinks he is wiser than a whole council of sensible advisers.
b: Meshivei ta'am are "those who return taste", people who give a discerning answer. Ta'am is taste, and so judgment (11:22, where a lovely woman has "turned her back on good sense"; 1 Samuel 25:33). Seven is a round number for completeness (6:31; 24:16; 26:25). Some think the seven are a king's council, like the seven advisers of the Persian king (Esther 1:14; Ezra 7:14). The lazy one is sure he knows better than all of them, so he will never change.
orig: מְשִׁיבֵי טָעַם (meshivei ta'am), 'those who return good sense'

a: Someone who seizes a dog by the ears
t: Grabbing a dog by the ears
p: A dog grabbed by the ears will bite, and you cannot let go. So it is with joining someone else's fight.
b: Dogs were half-wild (see 26:11). Seize one by the ears and it will turn on you; let go and it will turn on you too. Mit'abber, "gets angry" or "gets worked up", sounds like 'over, "passing by", which comes just before it: a passerby who "passes over" into rage about a fight that is none of his business. Many versions render mit'abber "meddles". The Masoretic accents attach "passerby" to the man, not the dog.
orig: עֹבֵר מִתְעַבֵּר ('over mit'abber), 'a passer-by getting angry'

a: Wasn't I joking?
p: A man who deceives his neighbor and then claims he was joking is as dangerous as a madman with flaming arrows.
b: Mitlahleah in 26:18, "madman", is a rare word for someone acting crazily. He shoots ziqqim, firebrands or flaming darts, along with arrows and "death". The comparison is deliberately extreme. Deception that is later passed off as a joke is not harmless, because the damage is done before the excuse is made. The saying aims at a familiar trick: lying or setting someone up, then hiding behind humor when caught. Compare the harm a false word does in 25:18.

a: when there is no gossip
p: Nirgan is the gossip or whisperer who spreads stories behind people's backs (16:28; 18:8; 26:22).
b: Nirgan is used only in Proverbs, always for the person who murmurs tales and stirs up trouble (16:28; 18:8; 26:20, 22). 26:20–22 is a small group: no wood, no fire (26:20); charcoal and wood feed a fire as a quarrelsome man feeds a dispute (26:21); and the gossip's stories are swallowed eagerly (26:22). The point of 26:20 is hopeful: strife needs fuel, and if no one passes the story on, it dies out. James develops the same picture of the tongue as a small fire that sets a forest ablaze (James 3:5–6).

a: like treats gulped down
p: Mitlahamim means something swallowed greedily. The KJV's "wounds" is a guess that misses the image.
b: This verse repeats 18:8 word for word. Mitlahamim is rare, but the related Arabic word means "to swallow greedily", and most scholars render it "tasty bits" or "delicacies". The image is that gossip is delicious: people gulp it down, and it goes into "the deepest rooms of the belly", deep into a person, where it stays and colors what they think of the one it was about. The KJV, following some medieval Jewish interpreters, has "as wounds", taking the word from a different root. The Greek has "the words of tricksters are soft, but they strike into the inner chambers". Both catch part of the sense, but the Hebrew picture is of eating.

a: Silver slag
p: The Hebrew reads "silver of dross"; regrouping the letters, with a word known from Ugaritic, gives "like glaze".
b: The Masoretic Text has kesef sigim, "silver of dross": a cheap clay pot covered with a shiny coat of silver slag, looking better than it is. H. L. Ginsberg proposed reading the same consonants as kesapsagim, "like glaze", from spsg, a word for a glaze or a glazing material that appears in Ugaritic texts. Many modern versions follow it. Either way the picture is the same: a smooth, shiny surface over cheap clay, like warm words over an evil heart. The Plain keeps the Masoretic reading, since it makes sense; see the variant.

a: seven abhorrent things are in his heart
p: To'evot are things God and people find abhorrent; "seven" means the hater's heart is full of them.
b: To'evah (on this word, see 3:32) is what disgusts, often what God detests. In 6:16–19 there are six things the LORD hates, seven that are abhorrent to him, and two of them are "a lying tongue" and "a heart that devises wicked plans". The hater of 26:24–26 has all seven in his heart. 26:24–28 describes the smooth-talking hater: he disguises himself with his lips (26:24), sweetens his voice (26:25), wraps his hatred in deceit (26:26), until it is exposed "before the assembly", the gathered community or court, and he falls into his own pit (26:27).

a: The one who digs a pit falls into it
p: A favorite theme of Israel's wisdom and psalms: evil plans fall back on the planner.
b: The psalms describe the wicked the same way: "He dug a pit and hollowed it out, / and into the ditch he made he has fallen" (Psalm 7:15); and "They dug a pit in front of me; / they have fallen into the middle of it" (Psalm 57:6). Ecclesiastes 10:8 and Sirach 27:26 repeat the saying, and Esther tells a whole story of it: Haman is hanged on the pole he set up for Mordecai (Esther 7:10). The pit may be a hunter's trap for animals, and the rolling stone a weapon or a boundary stone moved by stealth. Proverbs states the pattern as a rule of how God's world works (28:10; 1:18–19).

a: A false tongue hates the people it has crushed
p: Liars come to hate the people they have wronged. Dakkayv, "its crushed ones", are the liar's victims.
b: The first line makes a sharp observation: people tend to hate those they have harmed, perhaps because the victim is a living reminder of their guilt. Dakkayv is "its crushed ones", from dakhah, "crush" (Psalm 9:9; Psalm 10:18). Some emend to "its owners" or read the line as "a lying tongue hates truth" with the Greek, but the Hebrew makes good sense. The "fall" (midcheh, "a pushing down") of the second line is the ruin that flattery brings, whether to the one flattered or, in the end, to the flatterer.
orig: יִשְׂנָא דַכָּיו (yisna' dakkayv), 'hates its crushed ones'

a: what a day will give birth to
p: The Hebrew pictures a day giving birth; James warns against the same boast (James 4:13–16).
b: Mah-yeled yom, "what a day will bear", treats each day as pregnant with events no one can foresee. The saying is not against planning (21:5; 24:27) but against boasting as if tomorrow were in your hands (compare 16:1, 9; 19:21). James applies it to merchants who say they will go to a city, trade for a year and make a profit: "you do not know what your life will be like tomorrow... but now you boast in your bragging; every such boast is evil" (James 4:13–16, rendered from the Greek). Jesus' parable of the rich fool, who plans bigger barns on the night he dies, makes the same point (Luke 12:16–21).
orig: מַה־יֵּלֶד יוֹם (mah-yeled yom), 'what a day will bear'

a: Let an outsider praise you
p: Zar and nokhri, "outsider" and "foreigner", here simply mean someone else, anyone but you.
b: The two words often mark a real outsider or a foreigner from another people (on zar and nokhri, and the "strange woman" built on them, see 2:16). Here they are used for emphasis: let praise come from someone with no reason to flatter you, not from your own mouth. Self-praise counts for nothing; honor must be given (25:6–7; 25:27). Paul makes a similar point: it is not the one who commends himself who is approved, but the one the Lord commends (2 Corinthians 10:18).

a: who can hold out against jealousy?
p: Qin'ah is jealous passion, especially a wronged husband's; no one can stand before it.
b: Rage (chemah) and anger ('af) are cruel and sweep over people like a flood, but they pass. Qin'ah, jealousy or zeal, is more dangerous because it is fixed and patient. Proverbs uses it of the husband whose wife has committed adultery: his jealousy turns to rage, and he will show no mercy on the day of revenge (6:34–35). The Song of Songs calls jealousy "fierce as Sheol" (Song of Songs 8:6). The same word describes God's zeal for his people (Exodus 20:5; Isaiah 9:7), but here it is human and destructive.

a: kisses from someone who hates you come thick and fast
p: Na'tarot usually means "plentiful"; many versions, including the KJV, translate "deceitful".
b: The first line is clear: the painful honesty of a true friend can be trusted (compare Psalm 141:5: "If a righteous man hits me, it is loyal love"). In the second line, na'tarot comes from a root meaning "be abundant" (Ezekiel 35:13), so the hater's kisses are lavish and many. The KJV and others render "deceitful", linking it to a different root or guessing from the context. The point is the same either way: a flood of affection can hide hostility. Christian readers have long heard in this verse the kiss of Judas, who greeted Jesus with "Rabbi" and a kiss as he betrayed him (Matthew 26:48–49; Luke 22:48).

a: A full appetite stamps on the honeycomb
p: Nefesh here is the throat or appetite, not the "soul": hunger changes what tastes good.
b: Nefesh often means the whole living person, but its root sense is "throat" and so "appetite, desire" (as in 13:4, where the lazy one's "appetite gets nothing"). A stuffed person will kick away even honeycomb, the best food there is; a starving one finds bitter food sweet. The saying is about more than food. Plenty can make people ungrateful, and need can make them content with little. Moses warns Israel not to forget God once they eat their fill in the land (Deuteronomy 8:10–14).

a: so is a man who roams from his place
p: In a world of clan and land, a man away from his home lost protection, standing and support.
b: Life in ancient Israel depended on family land and kin, who protected a person, stood by him in court and took him in when he was poor (Leviticus 25:25, 35). A man who wandered from "his place", whether as a refugee, a debtor or a restless son, was as exposed as a bird out of its nest. The Greek makes this explicit: "a man is enslaved when he is exiled from his own places". For readers in exile later, the saying took on new weight (Psalm 137). Cain's punishment was to be "a homeless wanderer" (Genesis 4:12), with a word close in sound and sense to noded, "roams", used here.

a: a friend's sweetness beats your own counsel
p: The Hebrew reads "and the sweetness of his friend from counsel of soul"; its meaning is debated.
b: The first line is clear: perfumed oil and incense, used at feasts and in welcoming guests (Psalm 23:5; Luke 7:46), make people glad. The second line, umeteq re'ehu me'atsat-nafesh, can be read in two main ways. Taking me- as "more than", it says a friend's sweet company is better than one's own advice (the Plain). Taking it as "from", it says a friend's sweetness comes from heartfelt advice ("advice of the soul"), so that good counsel is like perfume. The Greek has a different line altogether: "but the soul is torn apart by misfortunes". The verse fits the friendship sayings around it (27:5–6, 10).

a: A neighbor nearby is better than a brother far off
p: Kin matter, but in a crisis the friend or neighbor close at hand may help more than a distant brother.
b: The verse is long for a proverb, three lines instead of two. Keep old family friendships, "your father's friend" included (compare 1 Kings 12:6–8, where Rehoboam ignores his father's counselors). Do not run to a brother's house in trouble, either because he lives far away or because kin can be cold when needed most (19:7). The last line generalizes: nearness counts. The written Hebrew has re'eh for "friend of", an older spelling; the reading tradition has re'a. Elsewhere Proverbs praises a friend who sticks closer than a brother (18:24) and a brother born for times of trouble (17:17). Jesus' parable of the good Samaritan makes the neighbor the one who acts (Luke 10:29–37).

a: Become wise, my son, and gladden my heart
p: The voice of the father in chapters 1–9 returns: a wise son is the teacher's best answer to his critics.
b: Most of 25–29 is impersonal sayings, but here a father or teacher speaks to "my son", as in 1:8, 23:15 and 23:26. The son's wisdom will give the father something to say to anyone who "sneers" (choref, taunts) at him. In a culture of honor and shame, a son's conduct reflected on the father (10:1; 17:21, 25). The address may come from an old scribal school, where "son" was the usual word for a pupil.
orig: חֲכַם בְּנִי (chakham beni), 'be wise, my son'

a: A shrewd person sees trouble coming and takes cover
p: This saying repeats 22:3, with small changes in the Hebrew grammar. The shrewd are the good kind of clever.
b: The two verses are nearly identical; here the verbs are joined without "and", which makes the line quicker. 'Arum, "shrewd", is the positive cleverness Proverbs wants the young to have (1:4; 8:5, 12), the same word used of the serpent's cunning in Genesis 3:1 in the bad sense. The peta'im, "the naive", are not stupid but untaught and easily led (1:4; 14:15: "A naive person trusts every word he hears"). They walk on into danger and "are punished" (ne'enashu, are fined or made to pay).
orig: עָרוּם... פְּתָאיִם ('arum... peta'im), 'the shrewd... the naive'

a: Take the garment
t: Repeated from 20:16: the garment as a pledge
p: Take a pledge from the fool who guarantees a stranger's debt, because he will not be able to pay.
b: This saying repeats 20:16. A man who "stands good for" an outsider ('arav, becomes guarantor) has made a foolish promise, and Proverbs warns against it again and again (6:1–5; 11:15; 17:18; 22:26–27). A creditor should protect himself by taking the guarantor's coat as security. The law limited this: "If you take your neighbor's coat to hold as security, give it back to him by sundown" (Exodus 22:26), since a poor man slept in it (Deuteronomy 24:10–13). In 20:16 the written Hebrew has "foreigners" and the reading tradition "a foreign woman"; 27:13 has "the foreign woman" in the written text. On her (nokhriyyah), see 2:16: here she may be any foreign borrower, or the dangerous woman of chapters 5–7.

a: it will be counted to him as a curse
p: A greeting shouted at dawn is a nuisance, or a flatterer's show; either way it backfires.
b: To "bless" someone was to greet them warmly and wish them well (Ruth 2:4; 1 Samuel 25:6). Doing it at the top of your voice, early in the morning, may be plain rudeness to a neighbor still asleep; or it may be overdone praise meant to win favor, which people rightly suspect. Either way the blessing is "counted" (techashev, reckoned) as a curse. Some read the subject as the neighbor, others as God; the Hebrew allows both. Compare the flatterer of 26:28 and 29:5.

a: a woman who picks fights
t: The quarrelsome wife and how Proverbs portrays women
p: These sayings warn young men about a contentious marriage; the book also praises the good wife highly.
b: The "woman of contentions" ('eshet midyanim; written Hebrew madonim, the same meaning) appears four times (21:9, 19; 25:24; 27:15), with a related phrase, "a wife's quarrels", in 19:13. Sagrir, "downpour", is found only here: the drip of a leaking flat roof in the winter rains never stops. The sayings are written by men for young men choosing a wife, and modern readers note that there is no matching saying about a quarrelsome husband, though Proverbs condemns quarrelsome men often (26:21; 29:22). Proverbs is not only negative about women: a good wife is a crown (12:4) and a gift from the LORD (18:22; 19:14), a mother's teaching is to be kept (1:8; 6:20), Wisdom herself is a woman (8:1–36), and the book ends with the woman of strength (31:10–31). Feminist scholars such as Claudia Camp have explored how these female figures shape the book.
orig: אֵשֶׁת מִדְיָנִים ('eshet midyanim), 'a woman of quarrels'

a: his right hand meets oil
p: The Hebrew of this verse is very hard; the general sense is that such a wife cannot be controlled.
b: Literally: "Those who hide her hide wind, and oil of his right hand calls." Tsafan means to hide, store or restrain. Trying to restrain her is like trying to store the wind. The second line may mean that oil slips through the fingers of one's right hand, or that the oil (perfume) on his hand gives him away, as the KJV has it ("which bewrayeth itself"). Some take the verse with 27:15; others read it alone. The Greek has "The north wind is a harsh wind, but by name it is called 'on the right'", that is, lucky. All translations are guesses.
orig: צֹפְנֶיהָ צָפַן־רוּחַ (tsofneha tsafan-ruach), 'those who hide her hide wind'

a: a person sharpens his friend's face
t: Iron sharpens iron: friction or friendship?
p: Today the verse is used for friends who help each other grow. In the Hebrew, sharpening can be hostile too.
b: Yachad, "sharpens", is used of making a sword or a tongue sharp (Ezekiel 21:9–11; Psalm 57:4). The "face" (panim) is the person as others meet him: his expression, presence and temper. Many readers take the verse as friends sharpening each other's minds through honest exchange (compare 27:5–6), and the Talmud applies it to two scholars who sharpen one another in the study of law (Taanit 7a). Others, like Fox, note that iron on iron is friction, and that the saying may describe how people provoke and harden one another, for good or ill. The popular reading is possible, but it is narrower than the Hebrew.

a: The one who guards a fig tree gets to eat its figs
p: A fig tree takes years to bear and must be tended and guarded; so does a servant's loyalty pay off.
b: Figs were a staple of Israel's diet, eaten fresh and pressed into cakes (1 Samuel 25:18). Sitting "under his own vine and his own fig tree" was a picture of peace and security (1 Kings 4:25; Micah 4:4). A fig tree needs years of care before it bears (Luke 13:6–9), and it had to be guarded from thieves and animals. The servant who "watches over" (shomer) his master's interests will be honored in the same way. Jesus' parables of faithful servants rewarded by their master make the same point (Matthew 24:45–47; Luke 19:17).

a: so a person's heart shows back the person
p: Literally "as water, the face to the face, so the heart of a person to the person": a reflection, but whose?
b: Ancient people saw their faces most clearly in still water. Three readings are offered. (1) As water reflects your face, your heart reflects who you really are: look within to know yourself. (2) As water reflects your face, other people's hearts reflect yours: you find in others the attitude you bring to them (compare 27:17). (3) As one face mirrors another in water, so one human heart is like another: people are alike inside. The Greek takes a fourth line: as faces are not alike, neither are human minds. The Hebrew is short enough to carry more than one of these.

a: Sheol and Abaddon never have enough
p: Sheol is the world of the dead; Abaddon, "Destruction", is a poetic name for its deepest part.
b: She'ol is the place of the dead, a shadowy underworld all go down to (on it, see 1:12). 'Abaddon, from 'avad, "perish", is its partner in poetry: "Sheol and Abaddon are in full view of the LORD" (15:11; compare Job 26:6; Job 28:22). In Revelation, Abaddon becomes the name of the angel of the abyss (Revelation 9:11). The written Hebrew here spells the word 'avaddoh; the reading tradition has 'avaddo; both mean the same. Death's hunger is never satisfied (30:15–16; Habakkuk 2:5), and neither is human desire (Ecclesiastes 1:8). The Greek adds a line: "Whoever fixes his eye is an abomination to the Lord, and the undisciplined are unrestrained in their tongue."

a: a person is measured by the praise he gets
p: The first line repeats 17:3. A person is tested by how he handles praise, or by what people praise in him.
b: Matsref (melting pot) and kur (furnace) refine silver and gold, as in 17:3, where the LORD tests hearts. Here the test is mahalalo, "his praise". It may mean: (1) how a person reacts to praise shows his character, since praise can make someone proud or careless; (2) a person's reputation is the test of his worth; or (3) what a person praises shows what he is. The Greek takes the second view: "a man is tested by the mouth of those who praise him", and adds a line about the lawless heart that seeks evil. The verse sits next to 27:2, on praise from others.
orig: וְאִישׁ לְפִי מַהֲלָלוֹ (ve'ish lefi mahalalo), 'and a man according to his praise'

a: If you pound a stubborn fool in the mortar
p: Grain was husked and crushed with a pestle in a stone mortar. Even that will not beat folly out of the 'evil.
b: Rifot are crushed grain or groats (the "crushed grain" spread over the well in 2 Samuel 17:19). A housewife pounded kernels in a mortar to strip the husk from the seed. The saying imagines pounding the stubborn fool ('evil, the fool who will not be taught; see 1:7) the same way, and his folly still clings to him. It is the bleakest saying in the book about this kind of fool: no discipline will change someone who will not change. Contrast 22:15, where the rod drives folly out of a child; Proverbs distinguishes the young, who can still learn, from the hardened fool.

a: Make sure you know the faces of your sheep
t: A poem for the herdsman, or for the king?
p: 27:23–27 is a little poem on caring for flocks. It may teach farmers thrift, or remind rulers that power does not last.
b: "Know the face" (condition) of the flock means watching each animal, as good shepherds did (Genesis 33:13; John 10:3, 14). The reason given (27:24) is that wealth and even a "crown" (nezer, a royal diadem, 2 Samuel 1:10) do not last forever, while a well-kept flock renews itself every season. Read on the farm, the poem praises steady care of living wealth over money that can vanish. Read at court, where Hezekiah's men worked, it reminds a king or official that he is a shepherd, and that his crown depends on caring for his people (Ezekiel 34; 2 Samuel 5:2). Van Leeuwen and others see it as the closing piece of 25–27, balancing the court sayings of 25:2–7.
orig: יָדֹעַ תֵּדַע פְּנֵי צֹאנֶךָ (yadoa' teda' penei tso'nekha)

a: nor does a crown go on from age to age
t: A crown that does not last
p: Nezer is a crown or diadem. Its mention gives this farm poem a royal edge.
b: The Hebrew is a question: "and is a crown for generation after generation?" The expected answer is no. Chosen, "riches", is stored wealth, and nezer is the diadem of a king (2 Samuel 1:10; 2 Kings 11:12) or the high priest's crown (Exodus 29:6). The word makes best sense if the poem has a royal reader in mind. The written Hebrew spells the last word dor; the reading tradition adds "and": "generation and generation". The meaning is the same.

a: goats to pay the price of a field
p: A household could clothe itself from its lambs, buy land with its goats and live on goat milk.
b: In Israel's mixed farming, sheep gave wool for clothing, and goats gave milk, meat and hair for tents and cloth. Male goats ('attudim) could be sold to buy more land. Goat milk, more plentiful than cow's milk in the hill country, fed the family and the household's "servant girls" (na'arot, young women who worked in the house and field, as in Ruth 2:8 and 31:15). The poem ends with "life" (chayyim): well-tended flocks mean life for the whole household. The Greek turns the last verse into a teacher's word: "Son, from me you have strong sayings for your life and for the life of your servants."

a: The wicked flee with no one after them
p: The words echo the covenant curses of Leviticus 26, where the disobedient flee when no one is after them.
b: Leviticus warns Israel that if they break the covenant, "you will flee when no one is after you" (Leviticus 26:17), and the sound of a blown leaf will chase them (Leviticus 26:36). Proverbs turns the national curse into a rule of the inner life: a guilty conscience runs from shadows. The righteous, by contrast, feel as safe as a kefir, a young lion in its prime (compare 30:30). The verb is singular in the second line ("he is confident") with a plural subject, a small roughness that shows each righteous person stands on his own. Chapters 28–29 are full of such contrasts between the righteous and the wicked.

a: When a land rebels, it gets many princes
t: Many rulers, or one wise one
p: A rebellious land has one ruler after another; a ruler with understanding brings lasting order.
b: Pesha' is rebellion or transgression. A land given to it gets "many princes": rapid changes of ruler through coups and revolts. Readers often think of the northern kingdom, where nine dynasties came and went in two centuries (1 Kings 15–16; 2 Kings 15), a history Hezekiah's men knew well after Samaria fell in 722 BC. The second line is difficult: literally "and through a man understanding, knowing, so (ken) it lasts long". Ken may mean "right order" or "stability". The Greek reads differently: "Because of the sins of the ungodly, quarrels arise, but a shrewd man will quench them."

a: A man who is poor himself and grinds down the poor
t: A poor man, or a ruler?
p: The Hebrew says a "poor man" oppresses the poor. Some change one vowel to read "a ruler" or "head".
b: Rash, "poor", is surprising as the oppressor. Some scholars read rosh, "head, leader", or rasha', "wicked", which would fit 28:15–16. But the Hebrew can stand: a poor man given a little power, or one who has clawed his way up, can be the harshest oppressor of all, because he knows no other way (compare Jesus' parable of the unforgiving servant, Matthew 18:28–30). He is like a beating rain that should bring growth but washes the seed and soil away. The BSB's "a destitute leader" combines both readings.

a: People who walk away from the law
p: Torah appears four times in 28–29 (28:4, 7, 9; 29:18). It may be the sage's teaching or God's law given through Moses.
b: In chapters 1–9, torah is often the teaching of a father or mother (on the word and its rendering, see 1:8). In 28–29 it stands alone, without "my" or "your mother's", and is paired with seeking the LORD (28:5), prayer (28:9) and prophetic vision (29:18). Many scholars therefore think it here means God's law, the teaching of Moses, as in Deuteronomy, which is in keeping with Hezekiah's reforms (2 Kings 18:6). Others think it means wisdom teaching in general, which Proverbs sees as one with God's will. Jewish tradition has always read it as the Torah. Either way, keeping the law means taking sides: those who keep it "take on" the wicked (yitgaru, contend with them), while those who abandon it praise them.

a: but those who seek the LORD understand it all
p: Justice is not only a matter of rules: those who seek the LORD understand what is right in every case.
b: Mishpat is justice, the right decision in a case, and right order in society. Evil men "do not understand" it, not because they lack information but because they do not want it. To "seek the LORD" is to turn to him in worship and obedience (Deuteronomy 4:29; Psalm 105:4). Proverbs ties moral knowledge to relationship with God from the start (1:7; 2:5–9). Paul makes a similar claim: the spiritual person judges all things (1 Corinthians 2:15).

a: one who twists his two paths
t: Better poor and honest: repeated from 19:1
p: The first line repeats 19:1. The double "two paths" pictures a crooked man who walks two ways at once.
b: In 19:1 the poor man of integrity is better than one with crooked lips who is a fool; here he is better than one with crooked "two ways" who is rich. Derakhayim is a dual, "two roads", also in 28:18. It pictures a double life: one road in public, another in private; or a man who wavers between paths (compare Sirach 2:12, "Woe ... to the sinner who steps onto two paths"; James 1:8, a double-minded man). Proverbs often says poverty with integrity is better than wealth without it (15:16–17; 16:8, 19; 17:1).
orig: עִקֵּשׁ דְּרָכַיִם ('iqqesh derakhayim), 'twisted of two ways'

a: the one who runs with gluttons disgraces his father
p: The "glutton" (zolel) is the son Deuteronomy calls "a glutton and a drunkard" (Deuteronomy 21:20).
b: Zolelim are gluttons and wastrels, those who squander food and money. The law describes the rebellious son whose parents bring him to the elders: "He is a glutton and a drunkard" (Deuteronomy 21:20). In 23:20–21 the young man is warned to stay away from wine-swillers and those who stuff themselves with meat. Here a son's company shows whether he keeps the law, and his choice brings honor or shame on his father (10:1; 29:3). Jesus' enemies called him "an eater and a wine-drinker, a friend of tax collectors and sinners", using the old phrase as an insult (Matthew 11:19; Luke 7:34).

a: interest and profit
t: Neshekh and tarbit: interest and profit
p: The two Hebrew words for interest stand together in the law (Leviticus 25:36); here the gain ends up with the poor.
b: Neshekh comes from nashakh, "to bite": interest that bites the borrower. Tarbit (or marbit) is "increase", profit taken on a loan of food or money. The law pairs them: "Do not take interest or profit from him" (Leviticus 25:36; compare Leviticus 25:37). Israel's law forbade charging interest to a fellow Israelite, especially one in need (Exodus 22:25; Deuteronomy 23:19–20), and the righteous man of Psalm 15 "lends his silver without charging interest" (Psalm 15:5; compare Ezekiel 18:8, 13). These loans were mainly to the poor in hard times, not business loans. The verbal play is clear in Hebrew: the man who "grows" (marbeh) his wealth by "increase" (tarbit) is only gathering it for someone else.
orig: בְּנֶשֶׁךְ וְתַרְבִּית (beneshekh vetarbit), 'by biting interest and increase'
r: Leviticus 25:35–37; Exodus 22:25; Deuteronomy 23:19–20; Psalm 15:5; Ezekiel 18:8; Nehemiah 5:1–13

a: is storing it up for someone who is kind to the poor
t: How does the money change hands?
p: Proverbs does not say how. It trusts that God will move wealth gained by exploiting the poor into kinder hands.
b: Several passages share this conviction: "what a sinner has built up is stored away for the righteous" (13:22); the wicked man piles up silver, "and a righteous man wears it" (Job 27:16–17); God gives the sinner's gathering to the one who pleases him (Ecclesiastes 2:26). The saying may picture an heir who is generous, a ruler who confiscates and redistributes, or simply God's hidden justice over time. Chonen dallim, "one who is kind to the poor", is the person praised in 14:31 and 19:17, who "lends to the LORD". The saying gives the lender a reason to stop: interest from the poor is gain he will not keep.
orig: לְחוֹנֵן דַּלִּים (lechonen dallim), 'for one gracious to the poor'

a: The one who grows his wealth through interest and profit
p: Jewish law kept the ban on interest between Jews and developed ways to allow business partnership.
b: The Talmud's laws of interest (Bava Metzia, chapter 5) forbid both open interest and disguised forms of it between Jews, and the Talmud brings this verse into its discussion of loans to non-Jews, which Deuteronomy 23:20 permits (Bava Metzia 70b). Maimonides counted lending at interest to a fellow Jew as a violation of several commandments at once. In the 1500s and 1600s, as Jewish trade grew, rabbis in Poland developed the heter iska, a contract that turns a loan into a business partnership in which the investor shares profit and risk. It is still used, for example by Israeli banks. The arrangement shows the same distinction Proverbs and the law make: the ban targets profit taken from a neighbor in need.

a: his prayer, too, is abhorrent
p: If someone will not listen to God's law, God will not welcome his prayer. The hearing goes both ways.
b: The saying turns on hearing: the man turns his ear away from hearing the law, so his prayer is unheard. To'evah is the strong word for what the LORD finds abhorrent (on it, see 3:32). In 15:8 the LORD finds the sacrifice of the wicked abhorrent but delights in the prayer of the upright. The prophets say the same: God will not listen to prayers from hands full of blood (Isaiah 1:15), and a psalmist confesses, "If I had looked with favor on evil in my heart, / the Lord would not listen" (Psalm 66:18). Zechariah 7:11–13 sets it out: they would not hear, so God would not hear.

a: When the righteous are glad, the splendor is great
p: Four sayings on the rise and fall of the wicked (28:12, 28; 29:2, 16) run through 28–29 like a frame.
b: 28:12 and 28:28 say almost the same thing: when the wicked rise to power, people hide. 29:2 and 29:16 add that when the righteous increase, the people are glad, and the righteous will see the wicked fall. Bruce Malchow argued that these "frame" sayings divide 28–29 into sections and show its purpose: it is a manual for future rulers and officials, teaching them how their conduct shapes a whole nation. In 28:12, yechuppas 'adam means people "have to be searched for" because they have gone into hiding, the same idea as "people go into hiding" in 28:28. Ordinary people feel the effects of bad government first.
orig: יְחֻפַּשׂ אָדָם (yechuppas 'adam), 'a person must be searched for'

a: the one who admits them and turns from them will receive mercy
p: One of the Bible's clearest sayings on confession: hiding sin fails, while admitting and leaving it finds mercy.
b: The psalmist describes both halves: "As long as I said nothing, my bones were wearing out" (Psalm 32:3), but "I did not cover up my guilt... And you, you lifted away the guilt of my sin" (Psalm 32:5). Modeh is "one who confesses", from the root used for thanksgiving and praise. The second verb matters too: mercy comes to one who confesses and forsakes ('ozev) the sin. The New Testament carries the same promise: if we confess our sins, God is faithful and just to forgive them (1 John 1:9). In Jewish tradition the Talmud (Yoma 86b) discusses this verse in deciding how specifically a person should confess, and Maimonides makes forsaking sin and confessing it the two parts of repentance.
orig: וּמוֹדֶה וְעֹזֵב (umodeh ve'ozev), 'and one who confesses and forsakes'

a: Happy is the person who is always afraid
p: Mefachched means fearing or dreading. The verse does not say what is feared; most take it as a careful fear.
b: Ashrei, "happy", is the word that opens Psalm 1. Mefachched is from pachad, "dread, terror", and the verse does not say what the person fears. Most readers take it as the fear of the LORD (1:7) or a dread of sinning that makes one careful, the opposite of the person who "makes his heart hard", like Pharaoh (Exodus 7:13) or Israel in the wilderness (Psalm 95:8). The Greek has "Blessed is the man who fears all things out of reverence". The saying is not praising anxiety but a tender conscience.

a: A roaring lion and a bear on the charge
p: A wicked ruler is a predator, not a shepherd. The poor have no defense against him.
b: Lions and bears were the most dangerous animals in Israel (1 Samuel 17:34–36; Amos 5:19). A good king was meant to be a shepherd (2 Samuel 5:2; Psalm 78:70–72); a wicked one devours his people like a beast. Proverbs uses the lion's roar for a king's anger (19:12; 20:2), and Ezekiel calls Jerusalem's princes roaring lions tearing their prey (Ezekiel 22:25). Daniel's visions picture empires as a lion, a bear and other beasts (Daniel 7:4–5), and 1 Peter calls the devil a roaring lion (1 Peter 5:8). The "poor people" ('am dal) may be a weak nation or simply the ruler's poorer subjects.

a: Let no one take hold of him
p: A man guilty of blood is a fugitive until he dies. "Let no one take hold of him": do not help him, or do not stop him.
b: 'Ashuq bedam-nafesh is "weighed down by the blood of a life": guilty of murder. He will flee "to the pit" (bor, the grave; 1:12). The law gave no refuge to a deliberate murderer (Exodus 21:14; Numbers 35:31: "Do not take a ransom for the life of a murderer"), and Genesis 9:6 sets the principle that blood requires blood. "Let no one take hold of him" ('al yitmekhu-vo) can mean "let no one support him" (do not shelter a murderer) or "let no one stop him" (let justice run its course). Cain the first murderer became a wanderer (Genesis 4:12–14). The Greek has a different saying here and adds another: "Discipline a son and he will love you" (28:17a).

a: will fall at once
p: Be'echat means "in one", so "at once" or "suddenly". A one-letter change would give "into a pit".
b: The man whose "two ways" are crooked (see 28:6) falls be'echat, literally "in one": all at once, or into one of his two ways. The Syriac, as reported in the NIV's footnote, has "into a pit", as if reading beshachat, which differs by one letter, and the NIV follows it (see the variant). That reading balances 28:10 ("he will drop into his own pit") and 26:27. The Plain keeps the Masoretic reading, which makes good sense.
orig: יִפּוֹל בְּאֶחָת (yippol be'echat), 'will fall in one'

a: The man who tills his soil gets his fill of bread
t: Repeated from 12:11, with a sharper ending
p: The first line repeats 12:11; the second turns "has no sense" into "gets his fill of poverty".
b: In 12:11 the man who chases empty things "has no sense". Here the same verb "gets his fill" (yisba') comes back in both lines with a bitter twist: the farmer is filled with bread, the dreamer with poverty. Reqim, "empty things", may be get-rich-quick schemes or worthless companions (Judges 9:4; Judges 11:3). The next verses (28:20, 22) also warn against hurrying after wealth.

a: Favoring one face over another is not good
p: Hakker panim, "recognizing faces", is the Bible's phrase for favoritism in judgment. Even a crust of bread can buy it.
b: The same phrase begins 24:23 ("Favoring one face over another in judgment is not good"), and the law forbids it: "Do not play favorites when you judge. Listen to the small one just as to the great one" (Deuteronomy 1:17; compare Deuteronomy 16:19). A judge who "recognizes faces" decides by who someone is, rich or poor, friend or stranger, instead of by the facts. The second line is cynical and realistic: people will sell justice for very little, a pat-lechem, a scrap of bread (compare Ezekiel 13:19; Amos 2:6). James applies the rule to the church: do not give better seats to the rich (James 2:1–9).

a: A man with a grudging eye
p: Ra' 'ayin, "evil of eye", is a stingy, envious person, not someone casting a spell.
b: In Hebrew the eye shows a person's attitude to others. A "good eye" is generous (22:9); an "evil eye" is stingy and envious (23:6, "a man with a grudging eye"; Deuteronomy 15:9). Jesus uses the idiom: "Is your eye evil because I am good?" (Matthew 20:15), meaning "are you envious because I am generous?" and speaks of a good and an evil eye in Matthew 6:22–23. Later folk belief about the "evil eye" as a curse is a different idea. The grasping man rushes (nivhal, hurries anxiously) after wealth and does not see poverty (cheser, want) coming for him. Paul warns that those who want to get rich fall into temptation and a trap (1 Timothy 6:9).

a: will later win more favor
p: The Hebrew has 'acharay, "after me", which makes little sense; most read it as "afterward".
b: The verse says the one who rebukes "'acharay" will find favor. As it stands, it means "after me", perhaps "one who follows my teaching", as a few interpreters have taken it. Most scholars read 'acharit or 'achar, "in the end, afterward", by a slight change, or take the form as an old adverb. The sense is clear: honest rebuke may sting now, but in time people value it more than flattery (27:5–6; 9:8).

a: That's no crime
t: Robbing parents and calling it legal
p: A son who takes from his parents and says it is no wrong is no better than a destroyer. Jesus condemned a like excuse.
b: The command to "Honor your father and your mother" (Exodus 20:12) included supporting them in old age. A grown son might take family property before his parents' death, or neglect them, and justify it. Proverbs is blunt: he keeps company with the "destroyer" ('ish mashchit, a man who ruins). Compare 19:26 (the son who drives out his mother) and 20:20. Jesus attacked the custom of declaring money korban, "a gift" devoted to God, so that it could not be used to support one's father or mother (Mark 7:9–13).

a: A man with a wide-open appetite
p: Rechav-nefesh, "wide of appetite", is the greedy person whose wanting never stops.
b: Nefesh again means throat or appetite (see 27:7). A "wide" one swallows everything, like Sheol, which "opens wide its throat" (Isaiah 5:14; Habakkuk 2:5). Greed starts fights (yegareh madon, the same phrase as in 15:18 and 29:22). The contrast is unexpected: not the generous man, but the one who "trusts in the LORD", who "will grow fat" (yedushshan), meaning he will prosper, as in 11:25 ("A generous soul will grow fat") and 13:4. Trust in God frees a person from the endless need for more.

a: The one who relies on his own heart is a fool
p: Modern advice says follow your heart. Proverbs says the person who trusts his own heart is a fool.
b: The verse follows 28:25 with the same verb, "trust" (boteach): trust in the LORD, not in your own heart. In Hebrew the heart is the mind and will, the center of thought and decision. Proverbs warns repeatedly against relying on one's own understanding (3:5–7; 12:15, "A stubborn fool thinks his own way is straight"; 26:12). Jeremiah calls the heart deceitful above all things (Jeremiah 17:9). The alternative is not to stop thinking but to "walk in wisdom", wisdom received from God and from wise teachers (2:6; 13:20). The kesil, the fool, here is the self-confident one.

a: the one who looks the other way will be cursed again and again
p: Those who give to the poor will not lack; those who "hide their eyes" from them earn the poor's curses.
b: Ma'lim 'einav, "hiding his eyes", is deliberately not seeing need (compare Isaiah 1:15, where God hides his eyes from those who pray with bloody hands; Isaiah 58:7). The poor whom he ignores will curse him, and Proverbs assumes God hears such curses (11:26; 30:10). The promise that the giver will not lack runs through the book (11:24–25; 19:17; 22:9) and the law: "Open your hand wide to your brother, to the poor and the needy among you in your land" (Deuteronomy 15:11). Jesus' parable of the sheep and goats makes care for the needy the measure of the judgment (Matthew 25:31–46).
orig: וּמַעְלִים עֵינָיו (uma'lim 'einav), 'and one who hides his eyes'

a: keeps his neck stiff
p: A stiff neck is an ox that will not bow to the yoke: the Bible's picture for a person who refuses correction.
b: Maqsheh-'oref, "hardening the neck", is the language God uses of Israel at the golden calf: "Look, they are a stiff-necked people" (Exodus 32:9). It was later said of Judah's last king, Zedekiah, who stiffened his neck and would not turn to the LORD (2 Chronicles 36:13), and Stephen used it of his hearers (Acts 7:51). 'Ish tokhachot, "a man of rebukes", has been warned many times. His end comes suddenly: "in a flash" he "will be smashed, and nothing will heal him", the same words that close 6:15, said there of the troublemaker. Proverbs gives the wise a long road of correction; for the one who refuses it, the end is abrupt.

a: a man who runs with prostitutes throws away his wealth
t: The son who wasted his wealth
p: Luke's prodigal son is accused of devouring his father's property with prostitutes (Luke 15:30).
b: The two lines contrast a son who loves wisdom and gladdens his father (10:1; 23:15, 24) with one who "keeps company" (ro'eh, the same word as in 28:7) with prostitutes and destroys the family wealth. The warnings of 5:8–10 and 6:26 are about the same loss: strangers eat up what a family has built. In Jesus' parable, the elder brother says of the younger, "this son of yours, who devoured your living with prostitutes" (Luke 15:30, rendered from the Greek). The parable's surprise is that the father still welcomes him home.

a: a man greedy for levies wrecks it
p: 'Ish terumot is "a man of contributions": a ruler who lives on heavy taxes, or one who takes bribes.
b: Terumah is something lifted off and set apart: a sacred contribution to God or the priests (Exodus 25:2; Numbers 18:8), or a tax.
