"A man of contributions" is most likely a ruler who squeezes his people with heavy levies, as Solomon's forced labor and Rehoboam's threats did (1 Kings 12:4, 14), or an official who demands gifts for his decisions (compare 15:27; 17:23). Justice makes a land "stand firm" (ya'amid); greed "tears it down" (yehersennah), like a wall pulled to the ground.
orig: אִישׁ תְּרוּמוֹת ('ish terumot), 'a man of contributions'

a: is spreading a net for his steps
p: The flatterer spreads a net for "his steps". It is not clear whether the net catches the neighbor or the flatterer.
b: The Hebrew "his" can refer to either man. If the neighbor's, flattery is a trap to bring him down, the way hunters spread a net for birds (1:17; Psalm 57:6: "They got a net ready for my steps"). If the flatterer's own, he is setting a trap for himself, the theme of 26:27 and 29:6. Many commentators think the ambiguity is deliberate: flattery harms both. On machaliq, "smooth-talking", see 26:28 and 28:23.

a: but a righteous man sings for joy and is glad
p: Yarun, "sings for joy", is an odd form; some read yaruts, "runs": the righteous runs free while the wicked is trapped.
b: The first line is clear: an evil man's own wrongdoing is a snare that catches him (compare 12:13). The second line in the Masoretic Text says the righteous "sings" (yarun, an unusual form of ranan) and rejoices. Some scholars suggest yaruts, "runs", which would contrast the trapped sinner with the righteous man running free, and fit 4:12. The Plain keeps the Hebrew, which makes sense as it stands: the righteous have reason to sing because they are not caught.

a: knows what the poor are owed by law
t: Knowing the cause of the poor
p: Din dallim is "the case of the poor": their legal claim. To know it is to take it seriously and act on it.
b: Yodea', "knows", in Hebrew is more than having facts: it means caring about and acting on what one knows. Jeremiah says of King Josiah that he judged the cause of the poor and needy, and asks: is that not what it means to know the LORD? (Jeremiah 22:16). The wicked do not "understand knowledge" (da'at) of this kind at all. The saying belongs with the king sayings of 29:4, 12 and 14 and with the law's demand for justice for those who cannot defend themselves (31:8–9; Deuteronomy 24:17).
orig: דִּין דַּלִּים (din dallim), 'the case of the poor'

a: Mockers stir a town into flames
t: Mockers set a town on fire
p: 'Anshei latson, "men of mockery", fan a town's anger into flames. The wise calm it.
b: The mocker (lets) in Proverbs is the scoffer who sneers at correction and at God (1:22; 9:7–8; 21:24). Here "men of mockery" are public agitators who yafichu, "blow on", a town, as one blows on embers to start a fire. The fire is metaphorical, civil unrest or a feud that spreads through a qiryah, a city. Isaiah calls the leaders of Jerusalem in Hezekiah's own day "men of mockery" who rule this people (Isaiah 28:14). The wise do the opposite: they turn anger back, as Abigail did with David (1 Samuel 25:23–35) and the wise woman of Abel did with Joab (2 Samuel 20:16–22).

a: there is raging and laughing, and no peace
p: The Hebrew does not say whether the fool, the wise man or both rage and laugh. The result is clear: no rest.
b: Nishpat means to go to law or argue a case with someone. The second line has two verbs without a subject: "and he rages and laughs, and there is no rest". Most take the subject as the stubborn fool ('evil): whether the wise man is angry or friendly, the fool only storms or sneers. Others read it as the wise man: whether he rages or laughs, he gets nowhere. The Greek takes it as "a wise man will judge nations, but a worthless man in anger is laughed at". Compare the advice about answering a fool in 26:4–5.
orig: וְרָגַז וְשָׂחַק (veragaz vesachaq), 'and he rages and laughs'

a: and as for the upright, they hunt for their lives
t: Seeking a life: to kill or to save?
p: "Seek the life" usually means to try to kill. Either the bloodthirsty hunt the upright, or the upright protect him.
b: Literally: "men of blood hate the blameless, and the upright seek his life." Elsewhere "seek someone's life" (biqqesh nefesh) means to try to kill him (Exodus 4:19; 1 Samuel 20:1). Read that way, the second line must mean the bloodthirsty also seek the lives of the upright, and the Plain takes it so. Some read "the upright care for his life" (protect the blameless one), giving a contrast, as the Greek does ("the upright will seek out his soul"). Tam, "blameless" (see 28:18), is the word used of Job (Job 1:1).

a: A fool lets out all his spirit
p: Ruach, "spirit" or "breath", is here a person's temper. The fool vents all of it; the wise calms it down.
b: Kol-rucho yotsi' is "he brings out all his spirit": the fool says everything he feels the moment he feels it. The wise man be'achor yeshabbechennah, literally "stills it in the back": holds it back and lets it calm. Shabbach is used of God stilling the roaring sea (Psalm 65:7; Psalm 89:9). The saying is about anger above all (compare 29:22; 14:29; 16:32), but it also covers any feeling poured out without restraint. Compare 25:28, where a man who cannot rein in his spirit is a city without a wall.
orig: כָּל־רוּחוֹ יוֹצִיא (kol-rucho yotsi'), 'all his spirit he brings out'

a: every one of his servants turns wicked
p: If a ruler rewards lies, his officials learn to lie. A court takes its character from the top.
b: Mesharetav are a ruler's attendants and officials. When the ruler listens to false reports, flatterers and slanderers rise at court, and honest servants either leave or learn to lie. The Bible's histories show it: Saul believed false reports about David (1 Samuel 22:6–19; 24:9), and Absalom's flattery won the people (2 Samuel 15:1–6). The saying fits the purpose of 28–29 as instruction for those who will rule or serve rulers (see 28:12). It also explains 25:5: "Clear the wicked from before the king."

a: it is the LORD who lights up the eyes of them both
p: Like 22:2, this saying reminds both the powerless and the powerful that the LORD gave life and light to each.
b: In 22:2, "The rich man and the poor man meet; / the LORD made all of them." Here the pair is a poor man and an "oppressor" ('ish tekhakhim, a man of oppression, from a rare word also found in Psalm 10:7 and Psalm 55:11). To "light up the eyes" means to give life (Psalm 13:3; Ezra 9:8). The saying works in two directions: it warns the oppressor that his victim's life comes from the same God, and reminds the poor that their oppressor will answer to him. Jesus says the Father makes his sun rise on the evil and the good (Matthew 5:45).
orig: מֵאִיר־עֵינֵי שְׁנֵיהֶם (me'ir-'einei shneihem), 'giving light to the eyes of both'

a: When a king gives the poor true judgment
t: A throne built on justice for the poor
p: A king's security does not come from armies but from fair judgment for the poor.
b: The king's throne "will stand firm for all time", the language of God's promise to David (2 Samuel 7:16). Proverbs ties that permanence to justice, as 16:12, 20:28 and 25:5 do. Psalm 72, a prayer for the king, asks that he "give justice to the poor of the people, / save the children of the needy" (Psalm 72:4). Isaiah's coming king "will judge the weak rightly" (Isaiah 11:4). Christians have read these royal ideals as fulfilled in Christ; Jewish readers have read them as the duty of every ruler and the hope of the messianic king.
orig: מֶלֶךְ שׁוֹפֵט בֶּאֱמֶת דַּלִּים (melekh shofet be'emet dallim)

a: Rod and rebuke give wisdom
p: Shevet is a stick or rod. With tokhachat, "rebuke", it means physical punishment joined to spoken correction.
b: Shevet is a wooden rod or staff: a shepherd's club (Psalm 23:4), a ruler's scepter (Genesis 49:10), a stick used to beat a slave or a criminal (Exodus 21:20; 26:3; 10:13). Here it is the rod used on a child, as in 13:24, 22:15 and 23:13–14. The verse joins it to tokhachat, rebuke or correction in words (27:5; 29:1). Proverbs does not soften this: it assumes beating is part of raising a son, as did every ancient culture whose instructions survive. A Late Egyptian school text (Papyrus Anastasi III, as reported by Caminos) says a boy's ear is on his back, he listens when he is beaten; the Words of Ahiqar tell a father not to spare the rod. What Proverbs adds is the goal: the rod and the rebuke "give wisdom". On how Jews and Christians have used and read the verse, see the next note and the chapter page.

a: a boy left to run loose
p: Na'ar meshullach is a boy "sent off" or "let go", like an animal turned loose to roam.
b: Meshullach is from shillach, "send away, let go", the verb used of turning animals loose: "Who set the wild donkey loose to roam?" (Job 39:5). A boy left loose has no one guiding or correcting him. The saying names the mother as the one shamed, as in 10:1 ("a son who is a fool is his mother's grief"), probably because the mother raised the young child (1:8; 31:1). It is a warning against neglect as much as a command to punish. The Greek translates "Blows and reproofs give wisdom, but a child who wanders shames his parents."
orig: וְנַעַר מְשֻׁלָּח (vena'ar meshullach), 'and a boy let loose'

a: Rod and rebuke give wisdom
t: The rod in Jewish and Christian teaching
p: Rabbis limited the rod sharply; Christians today are divided over whether the verse commands spanking.
b: Jewish tradition. The rabbis kept the verse but hedged it. The Talmud tells a teacher to strike a child "only with a shoelace" (Bava Batra 21a) and puts under a ban a father who strikes his grown son, since that tempts the son to sin (Moed Katan 17a). Maimonides allows a teacher to discipline, but not cruelly, not with whips or sticks, only with a small strap (Laws of Torah Study 2:2). Christian readers. Many conservative Protestants, for example James Dobson in Dare to Discipline (1970), read the rod sayings as a mandate for measured spanking, given in love. Others, like William Webb, argue that the Bible's rod was a stick on the back for older youths too, with no stated limit, and that the Bible's direction of travel points toward gentler discipline (compare Ephesians 6:4). Catholic and Orthodox teaching has no official ruling that requires or forbids spanking. See also 13:24 and 23:13–14.

a: Discipline your son and he will put your mind at rest
p: Discipline now brings a parent rest later; ma'adannim are rich delicacies, the treats of a royal table.
b: Yasser is "discipline" (on musar, see 1:2). The reward is that the son will "give you rest" (vinichekha, the root of Noah's name and of the rest God gives in the land) and bring "delights" (ma'adannim) to your soul. The word is used of fine food: Asher "will furnish the dainty food of kings" (Genesis 49:20). The Greek repeats the saying earlier as well (28:17a). Hebrews applies the principle to God's discipline of his children: it seems painful at the time, but later yields the peaceful fruit of righteousness (Hebrews 12:11).

a: Where no vision is given
p: Chazon is a prophet's vision from God. The popular reading, that people need goals and plans, is not what it says.
b: The KJV's "Where there is no vision, the people perish" is often quoted to mean that people or organizations need goals and plans. But chazon in the Bible is revelation given to a prophet: "The LORD's word was rare in those days; no vision was breaking out" (1 Samuel 3:1; compare Lamentations 2:9; Ezekiel 7:26; Hosea 12:10). Isaiah's whole book is called his chazon (Isaiah 1:1). And the people do not "perish": they "run wild" (see the next note). The verse says that when God's word through prophets is absent, a people loses restraint, and the remedy is keeping God's law. The Greek has "There will be no interpreter for a lawless nation". The modern motivational reading may be good advice, but it is not this proverb.
orig: בְּאֵין חָזוֹן (be'ein chazon), 'when there is no vision'

a: a people runs wild
t: Running wild, as at the golden calf
p: The verb para' is the one used when Israel ran wild around the golden calf (Exodus 32:25).
b: Yippara' means to be let loose, to throw off restraint, as one lets hair hang loose (Numbers 5:18). Its most famous use is at Sinai: "Moses saw that the people were running wild. Aaron had let them run wild" (Exodus 32:25). Hezekiah's scribes would know that scene; there the people ran wild while Moses was up the mountain receiving the law. The two lines of the verse then fit together: without the prophetic word, a people runs wild; the one who keeps the law is "happy" (ashrehu, as in Psalm 1:1). Prophecy and law appear side by side here, the only place in Proverbs that speaks of prophetic vision.
orig: יִפָּרַע עָם (yippara' 'am), 'a people is let loose'

a: Words alone will not discipline a slave
p: 'Eved means a servant or a slave. Here, in a household, it is a slave; Proverbs takes slavery for granted.
b: 'Eved covers a wide range, from a king's high official ("servant of the king") to a bought slave. In 29:19–21 it is a household slave, under the authority of a master who may discipline him. Israel's law limited slavery among Israelites and protected slaves from abuse (Exodus 21:2–11, 20–27; Deuteronomy 15:12–18; Deuteronomy 23:15–16), but it did not abolish it, and Proverbs, like other ancient wisdom, accepts it as part of household life (17:2; 19:10; 30:22). The point of 29:19 is that some will understand an order perfectly well and still not respond (ma'aneh, an answer or obedient reply). On how later readers dealt with these texts, see the topic page on slavery.

a: in the end it brings grief
t: Manon: a word no one knows
p: Manon appears only here. Guesses include "grief", "an heir", "ungrateful" and "a weakling".
b: A master pampers (mefanneq, coddles) his slave from youth, and "his end will be manon". The word occurs nowhere else. Proposals include: "grief" or "trouble", from a root meaning "to be sad" (the Greek has "he will grieve over himself"); "an heir" or "son", linking it with nin, "offspring" (the KJV's "shall have him become his son at the length"; compare 17:2, where a wise slave shares the inheritance); "insolent" or "ungrateful". The Plain gives "grief", with the Greek and many commentators, but the meaning is uncertain.

a: A man of anger starts fights
p: The first line is nearly the same as 15:18a; the second warns that a hothead commits many wrongs.
b: 15:18 reads "A man full of rage starts fights"; here the angry man ('ish 'af) does the same, and the "master of rage" (ba'al chemah, a hothead) is "great in transgression". Proverbs repeatedly ties uncontrolled anger to wrongdoing (14:17, 29; 22:24–25). James echoes the teaching: be slow to anger, for human anger does not work God's righteousness (James 1:19–20). Jesus places anger alongside murder (Matthew 5:21–22).

a: Pride brings a person down low
p: Pride brings a person low, and the low in spirit gain honor. The Hebrew plays on "low" twice.
b: Tashpilennu, "brings him low", and shefal-ruach, "low of spirit", come from the same root, and the Plain keeps "low" in both lines. Pride goes before a fall (16:18); humility comes before honor (15:33: "before honor goes humility"; 18:12). Jesus states the reversal more than once: everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted (Luke 14:11; Matthew 23:12). Mary sings of God bringing down the mighty and lifting up the lowly (Luke 1:52). The saying connects with the court advice of 25:6–7 at the start of the collection.

a: he hears the curse spoken and says nothing
t: The curse that calls for witnesses
p: When a theft was reported, a public curse was laid on anyone who knew and kept silent (Leviticus 5:1).
b: The law describes the practice: "he hears the public curse calling for witnesses, and he is a witness because he saw or knew something, but he does not tell. Then he will carry his guilt" (Leviticus 5:1). Micah's mother pronounced such a curse over her stolen silver (Judges 17:2). A thief's partner who hears the curse and stays quiet brings it down on himself; he "hates himself" (sone' nafsho), because he chooses his own ruin. The word 'alah is a curse attached to an oath.
orig: אָלָה יִשְׁמַע ('alah yishma'), 'a curse he hears'

a: Being afraid of people lays a trap
p: Charadat 'adam, "trembling before humans", snares a person; trust in the LORD sets him high and safe.
b: Charadah is trembling, panic. Fear of what others will do or think traps people into lies and compromise, as Saul admitted (1 Samuel 15:24) and Peter showed in denying Jesus (Matthew 26:69–75). The antidote is trust in the LORD. Yesuggav means "set on high", out of reach, as in a fortress; 18:10 uses it of the righteous who run into the LORD's name. Isaiah tells Hezekiah's people not to fear what this people fears, but to fear the LORD of Armies (Isaiah 8:12–13), and Jesus says not to fear those who kill the body (Matthew 10:28).

a: Many seek the ruler's face
t: Seeking the face of the ruler
p: People line up to see the ruler, but the ruling that matters comes from the LORD.
b: To "seek the face" of a king is to ask to see him, usually to win a case or a favor (1 Kings 10:24; 2 Samuel 14:24). The saying does not tell people to stop going to court. It reminds them that a ruler is not the final judge: "justice for a person" (mishpat 'ish) comes from the LORD (16:33; 21:1). In 29:13 and 29:26 the collection closes by placing kings, oppressors and the poor all under God. Compare Psalm 146:3: do not trust in princes.

a: The righteous find a man of injustice abhorrent
t: The last word of Hezekiah's collection
p: The collection ends with mutual disgust: the righteous and the wicked cannot stand each other.
b: To'evah (see 3:32) is usually what the LORD finds abhorrent. Here the righteous find the unjust abhorrent, and the wicked find the upright just as repugnant. The saying is a fitting close to chapters 28–29, which divide humanity into righteous and wicked again and again. It does not call for hatred of persons so much as an honest admission: the two ways cannot be mixed (compare 2 Corinthians 6:14). In the Greek, Proverbs 31:10–31, the poem of the woman of strength, follows directly after this verse.
orig: תּוֹעֲבַת צַדִּיקִים (to'avat tsaddiqim), 'abhorrent to the righteous'
